name: Rishi Mishra
zh_summary: (Reposted by @TheStalwart) @aRishisays explains why the Brazil election shock felt extraordinary: vital elections are rare when politics has centrist continuity, and upsets usually come from 60/40 setups, not 80/20; it is a binary, non reflexive event unlike the FOMC.
en_summary: (Reposted by @TheStalwart) @aRishisays explains why the Brazil election shock felt extraordinary: vital elections are rare when politics has centrist continuity, and upsets usually come from 60/40 setups, not 80/20; it is a binary, non reflexive event unlike the FOMC.
text:
Two reasons:

1. Elections that are this vital have usually been rare (getting more frequent now - think France, US, Canada last year, Brazil today). Most of the time elections don’t matter much for markets when there is some kind of centrist continuity to politics. 

2. When they do matter, upsets happen but typically from a 60-40, 66-33 setup instead of 80-20. 

Combined, this Brazil election becomes a huge surprise and hence feels extraordinary. But then again, it’s a binary, non-reflexive event (unlike the FOMC) so the odds don’t really have predictive power. It’s just a collective guess, and so expected to miss every now and then.

3) Hawks will also argue that policy isn't restrictive and needs to be

1) If officials still think this is a 2-3 hike recalibration, spacing out remaining moves costs little. "Being six weeks late is a manageable risk," says Rob Kaplan

zh_summary: @SawyerMerritt says SpaceX secured the largest GPU financing ever: a $40B master finance lease with an Apollo managed entity for NVIDIA Vera Rubin chips for its terrestrial compute buildout.
en_summary: @SawyerMerritt says SpaceX secured the largest GPU financing ever: a $40B master finance lease with an Apollo managed entity for NVIDIA Vera Rubin chips for its terrestrial compute buildout.
text:
SpaceX has officially announced that they have secured $40 billion in the largest GPU financing ever.

The company entered into a $40B master finance lease for GPUs and related equipment with an entity managed by Apollo Global Management. This lease will deliver the next generation of NVIDIA Vera Rubin chips for SpaceX's terrestrial compute buildout and is an important step in our plan to build a Super Intelligence future. It represents the largest committed GPU financing ever.

SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen:
"SpaceX aims to deploy the largest compute infrastructure in the world. As demand for compute continues to accelerate, we're seeing less than one year payback periods on our SI infrastructure investments. This lease diversifies our funding sources and addresses a notable portion of the funding required to deliver on our growth plans as we aim to get additional compute online at record speeds to power Grok for enterprises and consumers, as well as serve existing and future cloud services customers."

Transaction Details:
The financing has been committed to by a number of financing parties led by Apollo and Goldman Sachs, who served as sole structuring agent. Entry into the lease remains subject to certain specified closing conditions and is expected to close prior to year-end 2026, with lease schedules expected to commence upon delivery of GPUs and related equipment in the first half of 2027.

text:
6 PLAYBOOKS FOR 6 DIFFERENT MARKET REGIMES

Last week’s firm-wide @smbcapital meeting was about better adapting to different market regimes.

Which begs the question - what types of market regimes are there for discretionary traders? And what playbooks should we be running for each of them?

I’ll start and you all can expand on this in the replies.

Obviously this is far from exhaustive and kept high-level, but I think this should lead serious traders to do some deep reflection of their own. 

1. Theme-driven bullish market. Markets like this one favor momentum strategies, swing longs, overnight momentum, IPOs, and headlines relevant to the driving theme.

Early summer of 2026 certainly fell under this with AI as the driver and leading sectors like DRAM / cloud computing.

2. Macro-driven markets. Think in the spring during the start of the U.S.-Iran conflict, think  2025 Trump tariffs and the Russia-Ukraine war. Due to the randomness and volatility of these headlines, this market highly favors breaking news trading as well as trading move-to-move, while greatly reducing overnight exposure and swing exposure. 

3. Range-bound market. Think of the last couple months, where we've had no prevailing theme and most indices have stayed range-bound while the leaders from the prior cycle corrected. In this market, you want to reduce overall trading activity and risk allocation. If volatility is inflated, you might focus on selling vol, but you need to be careful of complacency. There

$META

META OFFICIALLY ENTERS THE CAPITAL RAISING GAME THROUGH SELLING MORE OF THEIR STOCK.

Meta announced plans to raise approximately $35 billion through two equity offerings:

- $22.5B in Class A common stock through forward sale agreements.

- $12.5B in depositary shares tied to mandatory convertible preferred stock.

The company is also considering a separate $60 billion offering program for its new nonvoting Class C shares, potentially beginning in Q1 2027. The nonvoting class was introduced on earnings last week and will result in a 2-for-1 stock split. 

The total raise so far will be around $95B, $10B more than Google’s $85B equity offering from a few months ago. 

$NVDA NVIDIA, $AMD, and $AVGO Broadcom have also expressed nonbinding interest in purchasing a combined $5 billion of Meta shares…which basically means the suppliers of chips to Meta will now be taking a direct equity stake into them. Meta already has warrants that convert into shares for 10% of $AMD if it holds above $600 in the future. 

Capital is now becoming the constraint…whoever can raise the most will win.

text:
Every dollar wants to be in AI compute right now

ARK Invest's Brett Winton on why that's making Bitcoin's "insurance" more expensive to hold

"Right now the world is basically sending out this giant emergency spinning beacon. All capital available needs to go into AI compute infrastructure, because we need as much as possible."

"Any asset that's not generating immediate great returns looks net worse on that basis. And so the cost of holding Bitcoin for this insurance contract has gone up."

"It's not just a Bitcoin and cryptocurrency issue. That is an issue for all businesses of all stripes all over the world."

"There's a black hole, and there's kind of like the tidal force that's pulling money into creating the infrastructure we need for superintelligence."

"Given the prospective returns of building data centers, it's clear that there's not enough money in that pool. And so it means that there's still this call on capital from everywhere else."

• EVs have their highest backlog in 4 years, with Musk adding that "...we are producing and delivering as many cars as we can...".

• High-volume manufacturing of Optimus is officially underway in Fremont, yielding the company’s first production-grade humanoid robots built on a standard assembly line.
• Energy storage demand is "very strong" with Musk adding "We're actually almost sold out of all Megapacks for 2027, and we're ramping production as quickly as possible to meet demand. We also expect gross margins on that to increase meaningfully."
• Not to mention recent launches of the Cybercab, Tesla Semi, and Roadster (with the latter unlikely to be needle-moving).

Call us biased, but between that conference call commentary and shiny new product drops, Tesla appears to be dripping with growth potential. Count us in."

George reiterated a $442 price target for $TSLA.

text:
Thoughts around AI

1) Given AI is the largest technology revolution in history at roughly 3.5% of GPD (larger than electrification, highways & internet combined); there is overinvestment due to the potential rewards for the eventual winners.

2) But much like during the Internet buildout, which had several large drawdowns including in 1997 (Asian currency crisis) and 1998 (Russian bond default), and then ripped higher, the question is whether this is THE TOP.

3) AI had 3 separate investment waves: training, inference and now Agentic
a. Agentic demands 10-100x more tokens than inference and started with OpenClaw in January for the tech savvy followed by Muse in late September for the rest of us.

4) Currently, the market is repricing two things
a. Financing costs are higher in both debt & equity mkts
i. Debt- $CRWV unsecured debt trading at 15%

ii. Equity- expected timing for AI related IPOs like OpenAI, Anthropic delayed earlier this year while filed IPOs of Firmus, AirTrunk, NScale, SB Energy delayed/ pulled

iii. Meta 8K “timing is important to secure capital before competitors saturate various funding options… in an increasingly challenging environment for raising capital.”

b. AI native growth rates slowing
i. Anthropic revs 145% q/q in Q2 to 45% in Q3

ii. Openweight driving ASPs down ~50% since May

5) Datacenter moratoriums seem to be the only thing both parties agree on
a. This could get worse after the mid-terms with a less AI-friendly political climate

text:
The US junk bond market is under severe pressure:

The effective yield on US CCC-rated and lower-rated high-yield corporate bonds is up to 18.0%, its highest level since the 2020 pandemic.

This figure has surged +500 basis points over the last 6 months, marking its largest 6-month increase since the 2022 bear market.

For perspective, this yield peaked at 45.0% during the 2008 Financial Crisis.

Meanwhile, credit spreads for CCC-rated and lower corporate bonds over Treasuries are up to 13.4%, the widest gap since July 2020.

Over the last 6 months, this gauge has risen +464 basis points, surpassing the 2022 bear market peak of 12.8%.

Cracks are widening beneath the surface of the credit market.
